frames.narration: The public subnet's route table has the local route and 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway. The private one has the local route and 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway. The database subnet has only the local route. That is the whole difference between public and private.

Baseline: web reaches the internet through the internet gateway, app through NAT, both reach the database over the local route, and the database reaches nothing outside. 4 working paths. A request to 8.8.8.8 matches only 0.0.0.0/0; the longest prefix wins in general.

Delete the NAT default route and app loses the internet: no route matches 8.8.8.8, the packet is dropped, and updates and API calls time out. Web still works because its public route is intact. 3 working paths.

Peer VPC B (10.1.0.0/16). With a route in A only, requests leave but B has no route back to 10.0.0.0/16, so replies are lost: still 4 working paths, and a hang. Add the route in B and web and app both reach B: 6 working paths.

If VPC B is also 10.0.0.0/16 the peering cannot be created, and 10.0.0.10 matches the local route, so traffic is sent to a host that does not exist in A. Overlapping CIDRs cannot be fixed with a route, only by renumbering.
A VPN adds 192.168.0.0/16 via the VPN gateway. The more specific route beats the NAT default, so on-premises traffic goes through the tunnel and web and app each gain a path: 6 working paths.

The trap: a patch has to be downloaded to the database, so someone adds 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway and a public IP. The database now has a path out and a path in from the internet. Nothing breaks, so it stays. Routing is the first gate; always check the second.
